title: Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
subtitle: The first man, the first caliph, the second of two in the cave
sources: Qur'an 9:40 — 'the second of two'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3665 — the Prophet's ﷺ words: Abu Bakr is from me and I am from him
Sahih al-Bukhari 3903-3906 — the cave and the Hijrah
Sahih al-Bukhari 1400 — his caliphate and the wars of apostasy

chapters.heading: The One Who Never Hesitated
chapters.body: When the Prophet ﷺ first called, Abu Bakr believed without a single pause — the first free man, the first of the ummah's leaders, and from that hour he never once stepped back. He bought and freed Bilal, Ammar, Umm Ubays, Zinnirah, al-Nahdiyyah and her daughter — the tradition names them — spending his wealth until his own house went without, and when the hijrah came, he was chosen: not for strength but for companionship. In the cave he entered first, searched the corners for scorpions and snakes, tucked up his garment to cushion the Prophet's ﷺ head, and whispered: if they look down they will see us. And the Prophet ﷺ answered with the verse of the age: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us' (9:40). He named him his companion in every generation's memory: 'Abu Bakr is from me and I am from me...' — the tradition preserved as: 'Abu Bakr is from me and I am from him, and he is my brother and my companion' (Bukhari 3665).

familyQuestion: Abu Bakr spent everything he had freeing people he didn't know. What would you empty your account for?

title: Umar ibn al-Khattab
subtitle: Al-Faruq — the one who separated truth from falsehood
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3680 — 'O Allah, strengthen Islam with Umar'
Sahih al-Bukhari 329 — the Hijri calendar and his justice
Sahih Muslim 2398 — 'the people of piety and excellence'

chapters.heading: Strength Given to the Truth
chapters.body: He came to kill the Prophet ﷺ and left his brother — the conversion the tradition counts as the turning point of Makkah. Umar's Islam was force itself converted into force for Islam: the prayer moved into the open at the Kaaba the day he joined, and the Prophet's ﷺ dua — 'O Allah, strengthen Islam with Umar' (Bukhari 3680) — named the rest of his life. As caliph he walked the streets of Madinah at night with nothing but his cloak, finding a woman baking with stones for lack of wood and sending firewood from the treasury with the words of the Qur'an on his tongue — amir al-mu'minin, commander of the believers, carrying the load the tradition captured in his own words: 'if a mule stumbles on the banks of the Euphrates, Umar will be asked about it on the Day of Judgment' (Tirmidhi 3700). He fixed the calendar, built the garrison cities, opened the registers of the conquered lands as endowment for the ummah's poor, and was stabbed at dawn prayer by a slave he had refused to harm. The Prophet ﷺ had said it of him in life: were there a prophet after me, it would be Umar (Tirmidhi 3686) — and Umar answered the sentence the way he answered everything: with tears.

familyQuestion: Umar carried responsibility for a mule on the Euphrates. What responsibility are you avoiding that is actually yours?

title: Uthman ibn Affan
subtitle: Dhun-Nurayn — the possessor of two lights, who equipped two armies and a standard
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3691, 3697-3698 — the two lights and the equipment of the army
Qur'an 33:23 — 'among the believers are men true to what they promised Allah' (revealed at the pledge of ar-Ridwan)
Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3701 — his modesty

chapters.heading: The Modest Millionaire
chapters.body: Uthman married two daughters of the Prophet ﷺ — Ruqayyah, then Umm Kulthum after her death — and earned the title no other man holds: Dhun-Nurayn, the Possessor of the Two Lights (Bukhari 3697). When the army of Tabuk lacked mounts, he equipped half of it — nine hundred camels and fifty horses — and the Prophet ﷺ said of him: what Uthman does today, no blame will touch him (Bukhari 3698). As caliph he completed what the previous two could not: the unification of the Qur'an into one master mushaf, the copies dispatched to every garrison city with the instruction that all variant readings be surrendered to it — the reason every Qur'an on earth today descends from a single archetype. He was besieged in his own house by men who had ridden his charity into Islam, and he forbade his household to fight: the Prophet ﷺ and I made a pact, he said — and he died reciting the Qur'an, its blood on its own pages. Modesty was his signature: the tradition records that he was never seen bare-headed, not from vanity but from shyness before the heavens (Tirmidhi 3701).

familyQuestion: Uthman equipped an army in secret and asked no credit. When you give, do you need the receipt?

title: Ali ibn Abi Talib
subtitle: The lion of Allah — first child to believe, fourth caliph, gate of knowledge
sources: Seerah sources: Musnad Ahmad 15493 — the feast of Abdul-Muttalib, 'he is my brother and my successor'
Sahih Muslim 2404 — 'I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate'
Sahih al-Bukhari 4356 — 'You are to me as Harun was to Musa'

chapters.heading: The Boy Who Slept in the Prophet's Bed
chapters.body: On the night of the hijrah, with assassins at the door, Ali ibn Abi Talib — barely twenty — wrapped himself in the Prophet's ﷺ green cloak and lay in his bed, so the killers would strike the wrong man while the Prophet ﷺ slipped away; Quraysh detained him, and he returned their trusts item by item before leaving Makkah on foot. He was the first child to embrace Islam, raised in the Prophet's ﷺ own household like a son — 'You are to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me' (Bukhari 4356) — and the tradition preserved the Prophet's ﷺ designation of him as brother, executor and successor at the feast of Banu Abd al-Muttalib (Ahmad 15493). The Prophet ﷺ named him the gate of the city of knowledge: 'I am the city of knowledge and Ali is its gate; whoever seeks knowledge, let him come to its gate' (Muslim 2404). At Badr he faced the champion Walid; at Khaybar he carried the banner the Prophet ﷺ gave 'to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger'; and in the pulpit of Kufa his sermons became the grammar of Arabic eloquence itself. The people of the house, the tradition says, are the boat of Noah: whoever boards it is saved.

familyQuestion: Ali slept in the Prophet's bed knowing swords were coming. What has your loyalty ever cost you?

title: Hamza ibn Abdul-Muttalib
subtitle: Sayyid al-Shuhada — the master of martyrs, the lion of Allah and His Messenger
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — his death at Uhud
Qur'an 16:126 — the verse that answered his mutilation
Sahih al-Bukhari 4043 — the Prophet's ﷺ grief over him

chapters.heading: The Uncle Who Became the Lion
chapters.body: When Abu Jahl insulted the Prophet ﷺ and a freedwoman told Hamza — hunting, still in his hunting dress — the uncle did not wait for deliberation. He walked to the Kaaba where Abu Jahl sat among his people, raised his bow, and struck him: will you insult him when I am upon his religion? — and the tradition records that some of Quraysh's own men wished, in that hour, that Hamza had kept silent long before. He embraced Islam the way he did everything: at full strength and without apology. At Badr he was the army's right wing; at Uhud he stood over the broken line until the spears found him. The Prophet ﷺ stood beside what the enemy had done to his uncle's body and wept, and said: I will mutilate seventy of them for you — until the revelation descended and forbade it forever (16:126). Hamza's title was fixed by that day: Sayyid al-Shuhada, the master of the martyrs. The seerah records the Prophet ﷺ seeing him in Paradise, walking on its rivers' banks, wearing two earrings — and the scholars said: he wears the mark of the wounds as honor.

familyQuestion: Hamza used his strength the day he heard his nephew insulted. What strength of yours is waiting for the right cause?

title: Bilal ibn Rabah
subtitle: The caller of Islam — the muezzin whose footsteps were heard in Paradise
sources: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3754 — Abu Bakr's purchase and freeing
Sahih al-Bukhari 1145 — 'Bilal, call the people to prayer' after the conquest of Makkah
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the first muezzin of Islam

chapters.heading: Ahad, Under the Stone
chapters.body: He had been the slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf, dragged onto the burning sand at noon with a boulder on his chest, and his answer was one word that has outlived every empire built on torture: Ahad — One. Abu Bakr passed by and purchased him — and the tradition records the exchange in detail, that Abu Bakr said: are you not content that he says Allah is my Lord and you have his blood on your hands? — and freed him that day (Tirmidhi 3754). At the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ sent him to the roof of the Kaaba with the words the whole city had waited twenty years to hear from its own stones: 'Bilal, call the people to prayer' (Bukhari 1145). Bilal climbed the House of Allah — the house his former master had worshipped idols beside — and called the adhan over a city of new believers. He lived on in Madinah as the muezzin of the Prophet's ﷺ mosque, and after the Prophet's ﷺ death he could not bring himself to call the adhan in the city again; the tradition records that he did it once for Umar, at Fajr, and that Madinah wept until Umar asked him to stop. His footsteps, the Prophet ﷺ once said in Paradise-vision, are heard ahead of him in Paradise.

familyQuestion: Bilal's one word under a boulder became the adhan over the Kaaba. What is your one word that could outlive your circumstances?

title: Salman al-Farsi
subtitle: The seeker of a thousand miles — the trench was his idea
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham — the long search from Persia
Sahih al-Bukhari 4190 — 'Salman is one of us, the family of the house'
Seerah sources: the counsel of the trench at the Battle of the Trench

chapters.heading: From Zoroastrian Fire-Worshipper to the Family of the House
chapters.body: Salman's road to Madinah took a lifetime: born to Zoroastrian fire-worshippers in Persia, he studied under a Christian bishop, was traded from master to master across Syria and Arabia, and carried at every stage one instruction from his teachers: a prophet is coming; his time is near; he will appear in the land of palm-trees between two lava-fields. When at last a caravan brought him to Yathrib — palms, two lava-tracts — he recognized the signs before he recognized the man: the seal of prophethood between the shoulders. The Prophet ﷺ heard his story of bondage and ransom and announced that Salman was not a client of any tribe: 'Salman is one of us, the family of the house' (Bukhari 4190). At the Trench, when the alliance of ten thousand surrounded Madinah, it was Salman — the outsider, the Persian — whose counsel held the city: a trench along the open quarter, as the Persians build. The Muslims dug by night through the cold; Salman supervised; and the tradition records that the Prophet ﷺ worked beside him on the rock, striking three times — and each strike split a third of the rock — until light shone from the rock of Madinah. The idea that saved the city of the Prophet ﷺ came from the farthest nation on earth from Arabia.

familyQuestion: Salman was a stranger with a foreign idea — and Madinah listened. What stranger's idea is your community dismissing right now?

title: Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah
subtitle: The trustee of this ummah — the man who pulled the Prophet's ﷺ own tooth at the Battle of Uhud
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 4078 — 'every nation has a trustee, and the trustee of this ummah is Abu Ubaidah'
Sahih al-Bukhari 3044 — the tooth at Uhud
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — his generalship in Syria

chapters.heading: The Pull of the Tooth
chapters.body: At Uhud, when the Prophet's ﷺ face was cut and a link of his helmet's chain was driven into his cheekbone, the companions crowded to pull it — and each, seeing his face, could not bear to be the one to hurt him. Abu Ubaidah took his own teeth — and the tradition records that he was the most toothsome of the companions, with teeth like a camel's — gripped the link, and pulled, and his two front teeth fell out with it. That image — the companion sacrificing his own smile to spare the Prophet's ﷺ face — is the whole biography in one act. The Prophet ﷺ named him in a sentence that outranks armies: 'every nation has a trustee, and the trustee of this ummah is Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah' (Bukhari 4078). In the wars of Syria, when the plague of Amwas struck his camp, he chose to stay with his army and die among them rather than survive by flight — and he died as he lived, in the line he had been trusted to hold.

familyQuestion: Abu Ubaidah gave his own teeth to spare the Prophet's ﷺ pain. What small sacrifice of yours would mean more than a grand one?

title: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
subtitle: The first to shoot an arrow in the path of Allah
sources: Musnad Ahmad 15492 — the arrow of Sa'd
Qur'an 31:14-15 — revealed concerning his mother, 'if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge'
Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3747 — the Prophet's ﷺ prayer for his supplication

chapters.heading: The Arrow and the Mother
chapters.body: At Badr, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas drew the first arrow of Islam and the Prophet ﷺ said: shoot, Sa'd — may my father and mother be your ransom (Ahmad 15492) — and the tradition counts that arrow the opening of every battle the ummah would ever fight. His trial was not on the field but at home: his mother Hamna swore to fast in the heat, neither eating nor drinking, until he left Islam, and the revelation descended on his case: 'And We have enjoined upon man goodness to his parents; but if they strive to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them' (31:14-15). The Prophet ﷺ taught him the dua that outlives every pleading: 'O Allah, I ask You for the word of truth in anger and pleasure, moderation in poverty and wealth' — and said of him: his supplication is answered (Tirmidhi 3747). He founded Kufa from a tent, commanded the armies that broke Persia at Qadisiyyah, and ended his life in the suburbs of Madinah, blind and old, dictating letters to the caliph Umar from his memory of the Prophet's ﷺ face.

familyQuestion: Sa'd's mother starved herself to pull him from Islam and the Qur'an answered his case. What do you do when the people you love most pull against your faith?

title: Talha and Zubayr
subtitle: The two who shielded the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud with their own bodies
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — their stand at Uhud
Sahih al-Bukhari 3694 — the Prophet's ﷺ praise of their generosity
Qur'an 3:140-143 — 'that He might test what is in your breasts'

chapters.heading: The Living Shields
chapters.body: When the line broke at Uhud and the spears converged on the Prophet ﷺ, Talha ibn Ubaydullah and az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam threw themselves in front of him — Talha taking blow after blow on his own hand until it hung useless, shielding with his body while calling out to the fleeing: come back, the Messenger of Allah is killed! The Prophet ﷺ said of Talha that day: whoever wishes to see a man walking on the ground who has completed his reward, let him look at Talha (Tirmidhi 3747). Zubayr was the first to draw a sword for Islam — at the very first confrontation in Makkah, the tradition says, he unsheathed first — and married Asma, the two-belted daughter of Abu Bakr, who ground grain until her hands blistered for their household. Talha was among the richest of the companions and among the most generous: the tradition records his caravan from Syria arriving in Madinah with seven hundred camels while the city starved, and the poor crowding his house, and his words: what family has none of it tonight? (Bukhari 3694).

familyQuestion: Talha's hand hung useless from shielding the Prophet ﷺ. What are you willing to take a hit for?

title: Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf
subtitle: The merchant of the ummah — who gave his garden as dowry and fed armies
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3675 — the garden given to Sa'd ibn Rabi'
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the caravan that came at Madinah's famine
Sahih al-Bukhari 1951 — his charities in Ramadan

chapters.heading: Commerce as Worship
chapters.body: When the Ansar offered to split their wealth with the Muhajirun, Abdur-Rahman ibn Awf answered: show me the market — and the tradition records that by the week's end he had earned and married, with a dowry of gold from his own trade, and Sa'd ibn Rabi' offered him half of everything. His genius was not merely earning: it was knowing whom earnings belonged to. In the great famine of Madinah his caravan arrived from Syria — seven hundred loaded camels — and he gave the entire load to the starving city, saying to the poor who crowded his gate: take, and beware of sin — he had not forgotten a single family of Madinah, and that night the market of the hypocrites was full of his flour (Ibn Ishaq). The Prophet ﷺ told him he would enter Paradise walking: the tradition preserves the sign — a dream in which Abdur-Rahman saw himself with footsteps of gold, each step stronger than the last, and the Prophet ﷺ said: it is your trail of good deeds (Bukhari 3675). He left, at his death, instructions for a caravan's worth of charity to keep flowing after him — wealth as a river, not a reservoir.

familyQuestion: Abdur-Rahman knew every poor family in Madinah by name. Do you know the names of the struggling people on your own street?

title: Sa'id ibn Zayd and Zayd ibn Harithah
subtitle: The tenth of the ten — and the beloved freedman whom Allah named
sources: Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — Zayd, the first freedman in Islam, 'adopted' then returned to his name by revelation
Qur'an 33:4-5 — 'call them by their fathers' (revealed for Zayd)
Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3747 — the Prophet's ﷺ praise of Sa'id ibn Zayd

chapters.heading: Two Names, Two Honors
chapters.body: Zayd ibn Harithah was kidnapped as a child and sold in Makkah, given to Khadijah, and given by her to the Prophet ﷺ — who freed him and kept him as a son until, years later, Zayd's actual father and uncles arrived in Makkah to ransom him home. Zayd chose: I will not leave this man for any people on earth — and the Prophet ﷺ took him to the Kaaba and announced before Quraysh: bear witness, this is my son, inheriting from me (Ibn Ishaq). When revelation later abolished adoption, Zayd's name itself became the test case: 'Call them by their fathers — that is more just in the sight of Allah' (33:5), and Zayd ibn Muhammad became Zayd ibn Harithah — the only companion whose name is carried in the Qur'an's own wording. He was the first Muslim slain at Mu'tah, and the Prophet ﷺ wept for him until his companions wept. Sa'id ibn Zayd, the tenth of the ten promised Paradise, embraced Islam at Umar's own hands in the house whose door Umar had come to batter — the brother-in-law whose home sheltered the recitation that converted a caliph.

familyQuestion: Zayd chose the Prophet ﷺ over his own father, then carried his father's name forever. What does that teach about love that costs nothing of honor?

title: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud
subtitle: The shepherd of Uqbah — more than half the Qur'an's laws come through his narration
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 243 — 'whoever wants to recite the Qur'an fresh as it was revealed, let him recite it on the recitation of Ibn Umm Abd'
Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3797 — the first to recite Qur'an openly in Makkah

chapters.heading: The Boy Who Learned Ninety-Plus Surahs
chapters.body: He was a thin shepherd boy of Makkah when the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr passed him at Uqbah, and Muhammad ﷺ asked him for milk the boy did not own — and the ewe that had no milk flowed, and the boy watched prophecy work before he ever heard a verse. Ibn Mas'ud attached himself to the Prophet's ﷺ household as a servant and a shadow, running errands and absorbing revelation until he memorized directly from the Messenger himself; the tradition counts him among the four from whom the ummah was ordered to learn the Qur'an: Ibn Mas'ud, Mu'adh, Ubayy, and Abu Musa (Bukhari 3808). When Makkah demanded: who will recite for us? — the companions knew the price of volunteering, and Ibn Mas'ud stepped forward: I will, for I am not a noble for them to kill, and I have no clan to avenge (Tirmidhi 3797). He recited Surah Ar-Rahman at the Kaaba until Quraysh beat him into unconsciousness — and when he woke, his first words were: what did the enemies of Allah do? The laws of inheritance, prayer, and purification that every Muslim practices today travel largely through his chain.

familyQuestion: Ibn Mas'ud volunteered knowing the beating was certain. When did you last volunteer first for something costly?

title: Ammar ibn Yasir
subtitle: The son of Sumayyah — driven from paradise to paradise
sources: Qur'an 16:106 — 'except for one who is forced, while his heart is secure in faith' (revealed for Ammar)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3798 — 'the pleased one, the one who pleases'

chapters.heading: Forced Words, Secure Heart
chapters.body: His mother Sumayyah was the first martyr of Islam; his father Yasir was killed beside her; and Ammar was stretched on the burning sand of Makkah until the words of unbelief were forced from his tongue while his heart held fast. The Prophet ﷺ wiped the dust from his face and told him the sentence the Qur'an then fixed forever: they forced you (16:106) — and Ammar lived with the verse as his shield for the rest of his life. At the Trench he worked until his own people could not recognize him under the dust, and the Prophet ﷺ wiped his face and named him what he remained: Ammar, the pleased one, the one who pleases — glad tidings, for the aggressors will kill him, and he will be calling them to paradise while they call him to the fire (Tirmidhi 3798). Forty years later at Siffin, fighting the army of Mu'awiyah, an old man was pulled from under the fallen; each side claimed him, and when they saw it was Ammar, the tradition records, Ali's men knew the Prophet's ﷺ prophecy had just been fulfilled — the rebels had killed him. The son of the first martyr became its most foretold one.

familyQuestion: Ammar's worst moment became a verse of mercy. What could your worst moment become?

title: Abu Hurayrah
subtitle: The keeper of the Prophet's ﷺ words — more narrations than any companion
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari — his narrations open the collection itself
Sahih Muslim 2493 — 'I was with the Prophet ﷺ and none was greedier than I for his words'

chapters.heading: Hunger and Memory
chapters.body: He arrived in Madinah with nothing — no clan, no property, no trade — and accepted hunger as the price of companionship: 'I would be overtaken by hunger and would fall on my belly on the road, and the people would say: the devil has possessed him — but it was only hunger' (Bukhari 6089). He ate with the people of Suffa, prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ in every prayer he could reach, and trained himself as a living archive, later explaining his unmatched memory: when the emigrants of Makkah were busy with trade and the Ansar with their orchards, I was free and hungry — I was present where they were absent (Muslim 2493). The scholars count more than five thousand narrations from him — more than any companion, male or female — and the Sahih of Bukhari opens on his authority. When the cats of Madinah gathered at his door, the tradition says, he fed them from his own plate rather than disturb them — and the scholars note his kunya, father of the kitten, was earned by kindness to the least of creatures. The man who memorized the most was the man who needed the most.

familyQuestion: Abu Hurayrah's poverty became the ummah's library. What is your limitation that could become your offering?

title: Anas ibn Malik
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ attendant for ten years — 'he was kind to me'
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 276 — 'he never once said to me even 'uff''
Sahih al-Bukhari 6039 — serving him was better than serving anyone else

chapters.heading: Ten Years Without 'Uff'
chapters.body: His mother Umm Sulaym brought him to the Prophet ﷺ as a boy of ten and said: O Messenger of Allah, Anas is a smart boy; let him serve you. He entered the household as an errand-boy and left it as one of the greatest narrators of the age — and his entire testimony of those ten years compresses into a sentence that has defined Islamic manners ever since: 'He never once said to me, even about a thing I had broken or a thing I had failed to do: even so much as 'uff.' And he never said about anything: why did you do it? — nor about a thing I had not done: why did you not do it?' (Bukhari 276). Serving the best of creation, Anas said, was better than serving any king, for by Allah, he never hit me, never struck me, never insulted me (Bukhari 6039). The boy who tied the Prophet's ﷺ sandals grew into the man whose narrations carry the sunnah of the household into every book of law — and his mother's wager, offering her son's service to the Messenger, became one of the most honored investments in the ummah's history.

familyQuestion: Ten years of service without one harsh word. What would change in your home if 'uff' disappeared for ten days?

title: Abdullah ibn Abbas
subtitle: Habr al-ummah — the scholar of the ummah, the interpreter of the Qur'an
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 75 — 'O Allah, teach him the interpretation'
Sahih al-Bukhari 143 — the Prophet's ﷺ prayer for his understanding

chapters.heading: The Cousin Allah Taught
chapters.body: He was thirteen when the Prophet ﷺ died, a boy who had crept close to every gathering — and Muhammad ﷺ, seeing him near, would call him close and make dua over him: 'O Allah, give him understanding of the religion and teach him interpretation' (Bukhari 143). The dua outlived the boy's youth and outgrew every expectation: within a generation, Ibn Abbas became the standard of tafsir, the man before whom the senior companions sat as students — Umar appointed him to the council of Madinah's jurists while he was still in his twenties, and the caliph said the people learn from him though he is young (Bukhari 4483). He taught that the Qur'an has four layers — the expression, the explanation, the lessons, and the rulings — and his method of reading each verse against every other verse became the grammar of exegesis for fourteen centuries. The Prophet's ﷺ house gave the ummah a dynasty of scholarship from a teenage cousin: the prayer of a dying man became a library of the living.

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ prayed for a boy's understanding and a library was born. Whose potential could your dua unlock?

title: Mu'adh ibn Jabal
subtitle: The scholar of Yemen — 'you are going to a people of the Book'
sources: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3095 — the farewell counsel and the Prophet's ﷺ weeping
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1327 — 'the most knowledgeable of my ummah in lawful and unlawful'

chapters.heading: The Judge Who Took Revelation With Him
chapters.body: He was the young Ansari the Prophet ﷺ sent alone to govern and judge the whole of Yemen, and at the parting the Prophet ﷺ walked beside his saddle for miles, teaching him the methodology that judges a million questions: by the Book of Allah — and if not found? — by the sunnah — and if not found? — then strive with your judgment, and do not shy from it, for the Prophet said: praise be to Allah who has enabled the messenger of the Messenger of Allah to please the Messenger of Allah (Tirmidhi 3095). Then Muhammad ﷺ raised his hands and said: O Allah, direct his heart and fasten his tongue — and the tradition records he wept as Mu'adh rode away, and when asked why, said: I fear for him the valleys' roads. The scholars count Mu'adh the most learned of the ummah in halal and haram (Tirmidhi 1327); he died young, in the plague of Amwas, and on his deathbed dictated to his students the jurisprudence of a lifetime until he could no longer speak — and they wrote with his breath. The student of the farewell became the teacher of the schools.

familyQuestion: Mu'adh was told: judge by the Book, then the sunnah, then your honest striving. What decision are you avoiding that honest striving would settle?

title: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman
subtitle: The keeper of the secrets — the man who knew the hypocrites by name
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3609 — 'the hypocrites are known to none but Hudhayfah'
Seerah: Ibn Ishaq — the pledge of the secrets at the Trench

chapters.heading: Entrusted With the Names
chapters.body: His father al-Yaman was killed by mistake at the Trench on the Prophet's ﷺ own order — and Hudhayfah, a boy in the line, was asked to forgive the commander who struck the blow, and he did, and carried the wound of it quietly for life. The Prophet ﷺ took him as a confidant: on the night of the Trench he walked the freezing lines with Hudhayfah beside him, probing for a weakness, and asked the boy — 'what do you say, son of al-Yaman?' — and Hudhayfah said: I say, we return to our families with honor or we fight behind you to the last man, and the Prophet ﷺ blessed the second (Bukhari 3609). Of all the companions, only Hudhayfah was entrusted with the roster of the hypocrites — Umar would cross paths with a man and ask: is he on the list of Hudhayfah? — and Hudhayfah's silence or answer moved governments. He outlived nearly all the companions, dying in the fifties of the Hijrah — the last keeper of a secret that died with him, as the Prophet ﷺ had commanded: the names went with him into the grave.

familyQuestion: Hudhayfah carried a list that could have made him powerful, and died with it secret. What would you do with a secret that powerful?
